name: Phishing & Social Engineering
description: Phishing, social engineering, disinformation, and human-targeted deception.

ccs.narrative:
Research on phishing and social engineering at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on phishing detection, social engineering, and online scams. Phishing Attacks on Modern Android (CCS 2018) set an influential baseline by showing how to Shows Android password managers and Instant Apps can be abused to launch convincing phishing attacks. Parallel contributions—"What was that site doing with my Facebook password?": Designing Password-Reuse Notifications (2018) and Data Quality for Security Challenges: Case Studies of Phishing, Malware and Intrusion Detection Datasets (2019) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. VisualPhishNet: Zero-Day Phishing Website Detection by Visual Similarity (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating Detects zero-day phishing websites via learned visual similarity to legitimate trusted sites. Other strong contributions included Catching Transparent Phish: Analyzing and Detecting MITM Phishing Toolkits (2021), Phishing URL Detection: A Network-based Approach Robust to Evasion (2022), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. TxPhishScope: Towards Detecting and Understanding Transaction-based Phishing on Ethereum (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Detects and characterizes transaction-based phishing scams targeting Ethereum users. Similarly, Content, Nudges and Incentives: A Study on the Effectiveness and Perception of Embedded Phishing Training (2024) and Characterizing and Mitigating Phishing Attacks at ccTLD Scale (2024) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

ndss.narrative:
Phishing and social engineering research at NDSS has addressed an increasingly broad range of deceptive channels. Towards Measuring the Effectiveness of Telephony Blacklists (NDSS 2018) set an empirical baseline by showing that robocall blacklists fail in practice, motivating subsequent work on robocall measurement and anti-spoofing (Are You Going to Answer That?, NDSS 2020). Simultaneously, link-preview deception in social platforms (Deceptive Previews, NDSS 2020) and e-commerce fraud via autonomous chatbots (Into the Deep Web, NDSS 2020) showed that social engineering was migrating from telephony to web and messaging platforms.

Double and Nothing (NDSS 2023) documented the anatomy of cryptocurrency giveaway scams at scale, characterizing an ecosystem that exploits social-media virality to amplify fraud. Like, Comment, Get Scammed (NDSS 2024) extended this analysis to comment-section scams on media platforms, demonstrating that social proof mechanisms embedded in platforms are systematically weaponized.

The most recent papers reflect the community's recognition that scam ecosystems evolve faster than defenses. Ctrl+Alt+Deceive (NDSS 2025) attempted to quantify user exposure to online scams across multiple channels, introducing a measurement framework that could track this moving target longitudinally. Throughout, the research has balanced measurement—how large is the problem?—with usable-security insights into why users remain vulnerable despite growing public awareness.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list pushed phishing and social engineering research beyond the classic email inbox. In USENIX 2018, "Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa" showed that voice assistants could be tricked into routing users to imposter "skills" through homophone confusion, while "End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks" (USENIX 2018) documented how weak email authentication still let spoofed spear-phishing slip past major providers. Together they framed the core tension of the area: technical channels keep changing, but the human at the end remains the target.

Around 2019-2020 the field shifted toward large-scale measurement and understanding why deception works. "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" (USENIX 2019) and "High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise" (USENIX 2019) moved detection inside the enterprise, where attacks come from already-compromised trusted accounts, while "Cognitive Triaging of Phishing Attacks" (USENIX 2019) and "Users Really Do Answer Telephone Scams" (USENIX 2019) brought psychology and human factors to the foreground. The two 2020 measurement studies, "Sunrise to Sunset" and "PhishTime," traced the full lifecycle of phishing campaigns and the real-world effectiveness (and gaps) of anti-phishing blacklists, establishing that the defensive ecosystem leaks badly.

The early 2020s brought a strong turn to visual and content-based detection, plus the cat-and-mouse of evasion. "Phishpedia" (USENIX 2021) pioneered deep-learning reference-based detection that visually matches a suspect page to known brands, a thread continued by "Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics" (USENIX 2022), "Knowledge Expansion and Counterfactual Interaction" (USENIX 2023), and the reference-list-free "Less Defined Knowledge and More True Alarms" (USENIX 2024). Meanwhile attackers adapted: "PhishPrint" (USENIX 2021) evaded detection crawlers and "PhishDecloaker" (USENIX 2024) tackled CAPTCHA-cloaked sites. A parallel line attacked the telephone channel, with "SnorCall," "UCBlocker," and "Combating Robocalls with Phone Virtual Assistant Mediated Interaction" (all USENIX 2023).

Most recently the field has pivoted to generative AI on both sides. "KnowPhish" (USENIX 2024) folds large language models and multimodal knowledge graphs into phishing detection, while "DeepPhish" (USENIX 2022) and especially "Malicious LLM-Based Conversational AI Makes Users Reveal Personal Information" (USENIX 2025) show AI itself becoming the social-engineering weapon. The area now spans automated brand-spoofing detection, telephone and robocall defense, and a growing concern that conversational AI can manipulate humans directly, returning to that original lesson that the person, not the protocol, is the soft target.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list (2018) approached phishing and social engineering as a broad measurement and detection problem spread across many attack surfaces. Researchers documented spoofing and impersonation in email ("End-to-End Measurements of Email Spoofing Attacks," USENIX 2018), abuse of emerging voice assistants ("Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa," USENIX 2018), mobile UI deception ("Phishing Attacks on Modern Android," CCS 2018), and the telephony channel, where blacklists and machine learning were first tested against scam and spam calls ("Towards Measuring the Effectiveness of Telephony Blacklists," NDSS 2018; "A Machine Learning Approach to Prevent Malicious Calls over Telephony Networks," S&P 2018). The unifying theme was establishing ground truth: what attacks look like in the wild and whether existing defenses catch them.

A major shift came in 2019-2020 toward studying the phishing ecosystem end to end and toward the human factor. Detection moved inside the enterprise with "Detecting and Characterizing Lateral Phishing at Scale" (USENIX 2019) and "High Precision Detection of Business Email Compromise" (USENIX 2019), while the human side was probed quantitatively in "Cognitive Triaging of Phishing Attacks" (USENIX 2019) and "Users Really Do Answer Telephone Scams" (USENIX 2019). At the same time the field began measuring the full attack lifecycle and the cat-and-mouse with blacklists, most clearly in "Sunrise to Sunset" (USENIX 2020) and "PhishTime" (USENIX 2020), with "PhishFarm" (S&P 2019) showing how evasion techniques defeat browser blacklists.

The early 2020s were defined by visual and reference-based detection and by analysis of attacker tooling. "VisualPhishNet" (CCS 2020) and "Phishpedia" (USENIX 2021) reframed detection as matching a page's visual identity against known brands, a line extended by "Inferring Phishing Intention via Webpage Appearance and Dynamics" (USENIX 2022) and "Knowledge Expansion and Counterfactual Interaction" (USENIX 2023). In parallel, researchers dissected the supply side of phishing, from off-the-shelf kits ("Catching Phishers By Their Bait," USENIX 2021) to real-time man-in-the-middle toolkits that defeat 2FA ("Catching Transparent Phish," CCS 2021) and crawler-evading reconnaissance ("PhishPrint," USENIX 2021). The deception lens also widened beyond classic phishing to survey scams, Zoombombing, SMS spam, cryptocurrency giveaway and Ethereum transaction scams, fraudulent e-commerce, and state-sponsored trolls and deepfake profiles ("TrollMagnifier," S&P 2022; "DeepPhish," USENIX 2022).

Most recently the field has turned to large language models on both sides of the conflict. LLMs now power detection by injecting brand knowledge ("KnowPhish," USENIX 2024) and removing the need for fixed reference lists ("Less Defined Knowledge and More True Alarms," USENIX 2024), while also serving as an offensive tool ("From Chatbots to Phishbots?," S&P 2024). Alongside this, the area has circled back to its human and organizational roots with large rigorous field studies questioning whether training even works ("Phishing in Organizations," S&P 2022; "Understanding the Efficacy of Phishing Training in Practice," S&P 2025), leaving the discipline split between ever-smarter automated detectors and a sober reckoning with the limits of teaching users not to click.
